query: Which pilot data sources or published studies provide empirical estimates for sd(log export), ICCs, and baseline survival rates needed to recompute sample sizes and set reestimation rules?

response.query: Which pilot data sources or published studies provide empirical estimates for sd(log export), ICCs, and baseline survival rates needed to recompute sample sizes and set reestimation rules?
response.answer: Empirical estimates for sd(log export), ICCs, and baseline survival rates can be found in published studies on cluster-randomized trials, primary care trials, and grouped survival data studies, respectively. These estimates help recompute sample sizes and set reestimation rules.

results.title: A Guide to Sample Size for Pilot Studies
results.content: ## **Sample Size for Pilot Studies** Maximising the value of pilot data. * Explore advanced methods that integrate pilot study objectives and design to calculate appropriate sample sizes. * Learn about internal pilot designs that allow for sample size adjustments based on interim data without unblinding the study. Newer methods allow for the pilot study sample size to be calculated, which integrates the pilot study's objectives and design. For example, the internal pilot design for sample size re-estimation can adjust for over-optimism in the estimates for nuisance parameters such as the variance or overdispersion at the planning stage. A well-conducted pilot study reduces the risk of costly design flaws in the full trial while ensuring that assumptions about sample size and study logistics are realistic. Unlike full-scale trials, sample size in pilot studies is not based on traditional power calculations. #### Internal Pilot Studies and Sample Size Re-estimation. Internal pilot studies allow researchers to adjust sample size estimates within a study without compromising integrity.

results.title: Intraclass correlation coefficients for weight loss cluster randomized trials in primary care: The PROPEL trial
results.content: The aim of this study was to compute intra-class correlations (ICCs) for weight-related and patient-reported outcomes in a cluster randomized clinical trial (cRCT) for weight loss. The proper design of a cRCT requires estimates of the ICC, which are often obtained from published studies.11 Indeed, the CONSORT extension to cRCTs calls for reporting the ICC for each primary outcome.12 Estimates of ICCs have been published for a variety of outcomes and for different settings (communities, schools, worksites, and medical clinics).7 Primary care remains the cornerstone of medical care in the United States; thus, primary care clinics are an important setting for pragmatic trials. ICCs have been reported for primary care trials for binary and continuous clinical outcomes and process of care measures.13–17 Despite using data from cRCTs (longitudinal designs), four of these studies used baseline data only to compute the ICCs.13–15,17 This approach limits the usefulness of the computed ICCs in informing sample size estimates for interventions where the outcomes are expressed as changes from baseline (e.g., changes in risk factors), or follow-up values (sometimes adjusted for baseline values). Adams and colleagues re-analyzed data from 31 cluster-based studies in primary care to compute ICCs for multiple outcomes.18 Most of the data were cross-sectional, with the exception of baseline and follow-up data from 12 studies; however, ICCs were not computed for changes over time, nor for specific variables.18 Therefore, there is a need to report ICCs based on longitudinal analyses of cRCTs to properly estimate sample sizes for future studies. However, these comparisons of cross-sectional results highlight the variability in ICCs derived in different contexts, and support the contention that the design of future studies should be based on data from similar populations (i.e., sex, age, race, socioeconomic status, etc.) in similar contexts (i.e., primary care, specialty clinics, community health centers, etc.). * In order to account for the clustering of patients within groups, estimates of intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) are often used to inform sample size requirements when designing cluster-randomized trials. * This study extends the results of previous studies by presenting ICCs for several weight-related outcomes, cardiometabolic risk factors, and patient-reported outcomes derived from a large cluster-randomized weight loss trial conducted in primary care.

results.title: Sample Size Reestimation by Bayesian Prediction | Request PDF
results.content: We review a Bayesian predictive approach for interim data monitoring and propose its application to interim sample size reestimation for clinical trials. In this paper we propose a predictive Bayesian approach to sample size determination and re-estimation in clinical trials, in the presence of multiple sources of prior information. 10 However, methods that use an interim assessment of the treatment effect to determine the final sample size of the trial have been proposed, [11][12][13][14] which include methods based on conditional power and predictive power. We propose a hybrid classical and Bayesian method to formally integrate prior beliefs about the study parameters and the results observed from an internal pilot study into the sample size re-estimation of a two-stage study design. In this paper we propose a predictive Bayesian approach to sample size determination (SSD) and re-estimation in clinical trials, in the presence of multiple sources of prior information.

results.title: Sample size justification in feasibility studies: moving beyond published guidance | Pilot and Feasibility Studies
results.content: This has led to many feasibility studies justifying sample sizes based on pragmatic reasons (e.g., the ability to complete) or on published guidance and various rules of thumb. We argue that feasibility studies should be designed for, or at least report relevant operating characteristics, specifically, the probability of determining a future trial will be feasible when it is and the probability of determining a trial will be feasible when it is not and that sample size justifications should be based on these operating characteristics whenever possible. There are obvious differences between feasibility studies and RCTs, including the objectives, available resources and acceptable error rates; nevertheless, the sample sizes for feasibility studies should also be sufficient to address their objectives at an acceptable rate and therefore, the justification of the sample sizes should provide some assurance that there is a high probability of making the correct determination of whether a future trial is feasible. Many authors have provided minimum sample size guidance and rules of thumb for external pilot and feasibility studies based on estimating the standard deviation to power a future trial, including Julious [4] who suggested 12 per arm, Teare et al. Unless other justification is provided it is not clear that guidance or rules of thumb will provide sufficient sample sizes for feasibility studies with multiple outcomes of interest. Therefore, if feasibility is the primary outcome of a pilot or feasibility study, and feasibility can be formally assessed by one or more methods, then it seems to follow that the sample size should be justified based at least in part on the operating characteristics the analysis method provides. To make good decisions at the end of a feasibility study, the progression criteria, analysis plan, and sample size need to be carefully considered and tailored to the specific objectives of the trial. Our suggestions for improving the design, and specifically the sample size justification, for feasibility studies closely mirror what is routinely done for RCTs. In an RCT, a typical approach is to first define the primary outcome and select a meaningful effect size and then to choose an analysis plan. It is time for researchers to move beyond the simple use of published guidance for feasibility studies, and instead justify the sample size of their specific trial.

results.title: Sample size calculation for studies with grouped survival data - PMC
results.content: Motivated by studies in HIV trials, cancer trials and in vitro experiments to study drug toxicity, we develop a sample size formula for studies with grouped survival endpoints that use the method of Prentice and Gloeckler for comparing two arms under the proportional hazards assumption. The sample size formula only requires estimates of the hazard ratio and survival probabilities of the event time of interest and the censoring time at the endpoints of the grouping intervals for one of the two arms. Inoue and Parmigiani8 and Raab et al9 discussed the design of such trials but focused on the design of follow-up intervals based on parametric models for the survival time instead of sample size determination for group comparisons. We derive a sample size formula for clinical trials with grouped survival data, based on the Wald test for the logarithm of the hazard ratio in a proportional hazards model and the method of Prentice and Gloeckler for data analysis. Finally, compared with the sample size calculation in trials with right censored data, we only need estimates of the baseline survival distribution at the finite number of visit times instead of the whole survival curve, which is due to the grouped nature of the data. By the aforementioned formula, we can determine the sample size if we have estimates of the effect size *β*, the distribution function of the survival time in the control group (*Z* = 0) and the distribution of the censoring time, both at the endpoints of the intervals. If we assume 15% lost to follow-up before the last visit time (36 month), which is the case in the trial in the work of Flynn et al,11 and if we assume the 15% lost to follow-up is uniformly distributed in 0, 36), then the sample sizes needed are 232 and 310, for a power of 0.8 and 0.9, with equal randomization, and these numbers become 218 and 291, if the randomization probability is 2∕3 for the vaccine group. To calculate the sample size, only estimates of the hazard ratio and the distributions of the survival time and censoring time at the endpoints of the grouping intervals are needed.
